Cruising high above dense Ukrainian forest, the combat drone spotted the long Russian column winding down the road from the Belarusian border. Its pilot, operating from afar, used the on-board cameras to scan the treeline for signs of anti-aircraft defences, then selected his target.
The bombs struck the spine of the column and one after another the fuel tankers erupted in a chain reaction of fireballs that illuminated his screen. “I think this was my greatest achievement,” the pilot, with the call sign Odesa, told The Times. “It stopped the offensive in the Chernihiv and Kyiv directions because the enemy had equipment but no fuel.”
The Times and The Sunday Times have teams of journalists on the ground in Ukraine and Russia, sending breaking news reports, dispatches, exclusive pictures and videos. Below are maps detailing the areas of Ukraine under Russian control and some of the most striking pictures and videos of the conflict from recent days.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/peter-r.title: Peter Reed: Life in wheelchair does not spell heartache for colossus who lives life on the bright side
https://www.thetimes.com/article/peter-r.text:
On the start line of the coxless four final at the London 2012 Olympics, Peter Reed heard a roar from the crowd echo 2,000 metres down the lake, filling his ears and his spirit. It felt like the entire nation was cheering on the British crew.
Sitting there with oar in hand, Reed could not have been in a better state. Physically, this 6ft 6ins colossus of superhuman power and endurance had never felt stronger. Mentally, he felt invincible. “Forgive the apparent lack of humility,” Reed says, “but sitting on the start line, I felt sorry for the other boats.”
Lieutenant Commander Reed had pity for his rivals, which felt fully justified over the subsequent six minutes — and seems all the more poignant as, ten years on, he cradles his gold medal sitting in a wheelchair in a London hotel. Then he was the epitome of athletic prowess; now he has to summon all his strength and will just to lift one foot a couple of inches to nudge a table leg. Life has been transformed by a catastrophic spinal stroke, but if you thought, as I did, that it might be difficult, painful even, for Reed to return to that time when he felt indomitable, his response is disarming in its equanimity.
“Thank goodness I did what I could when I could,” he says, of looking back to the glory days — which he did, quite literally, during lockdown when the BBC showed a rerun of that final and once more he felt himself inside a boat flying across water, barely able to hear the splash of the blades or even his own voice barking instructions as a crowd roared his crew to victory on Dorney Lake.
“Knowing it was going to hurt but that was fine, too,” Reed says, of the sense of perfect harmony and teamwork. “One of those days when you are right on the red line from the start, knowing and trusting that everyone is fully committed to every stroke.”
How was it to relive that? “I was looking down at my legs, thinking, ‘God, they were strong legs’,” Reed says. “I am proud of what we did that day and also grateful. How lucky I was to have done as much as I could possibly do with my legs before the time came when I could not use them. A lifetime of use into 37 years.
“So it’s not painful to watch now sitting in a wheelchair knowing I can’t do it again. At least I did it. When I finished rowing, I grabbed a motorbike and went around Europe for three weeks. Things get taken from all of us. It’s about living without regrets.”
As The Times reflects on a decade since that extraordinary, joyous summer when a nation came together, Reed felt like a man who, better than most, might be able to put it in some perspective. He has always been good company but, he thinks, even more so since his spinal stroke. More considerate, sensitive, available.
If London 2012 was the best of days, the worst came in September 2019, when he was at Okehampton camp on Dartmoor with an army commando group. This naval officer was fit, strong and flying, but felt poorly on an assault course. His gait changed with numbness and then pins and needles.
The excruciating pain which followed was traumatic evidence of a suspected fibrocartilaginous embolism (FCE) — a sudden blocking of an artery that occurs in the spinal cord — that is sometimes known as surfer’s spine. “The doctor said we will know for certain with an autopsy,” Reed smiles, grimly. “Sad, bad luck,” he adds. “But I was doing exactly what I wanted to be doing.”
The embolism was right in the middle of his spine, which means that he lost use of his legs and has no core strength. “But then two vertebrae higher and I would struggle to use my arms,” he says.
The journey since has taught Reed as much about life as has three Olympic gold medals and a career in the Royal Navy. There was the first attempt to board a bus in a wheelchair, almost ending up flat on his face, and seeing two old ladies vacate the disabled area for him. “That’s a hard day,” he says. “That’s when you think, ‘Ah, ok, that’s where I rank now’.”
Reed went to an Ed Sheeran concert recently and was greeted by one woman, saying, ‘Isn’t it wonderful you can be here’. “That pity and fuss,” Reed says, grimacing. It is a solitary note of frustration despite the challenges which involve four-to-six hours of “spinal-cord stuff”, as Reed puts it.
“Just going to the bathroom, showering and getting dressed at each end of the day is two-to-three hours. My digestive system does not work in the same way, bladder, bowels, there is plumbing involved.”
He is not burning calories in a wheelchair so uses a SkiErg. He wants to maintain strength to be able to lift himself in and out of his car, which involves weights. Using the monkey bars on a climbing frame is also necessary to straighten his hamstrings and hip flexors and avoid being stuck at 90 degrees.
It all adds up, and Reed is determined to keep as much independence as he can. He was married to Jeannie last year and they are looking for a home in Dorset which can be converted for his disability. “She has never had to help me go to the bathroom,” he says, “and I want it to stay that way for decades.”
His commitment is characteristic but, inevitably, there are significant compromises, including the medical discharge he recently accepted from the Royal Navy. He had been working to help the service with professional ethics and standards, but it was increasingly hard to make a desk job compatible with all his rehab. These days Reed, 40, lectures on resilience — his specialist subject — and is considering writing a book.
He has been approached to contribute to lobbying around attitudes to disability. He certainly understands how it changes someone. How? “Everyone can see my vulnerability, which means that, much more than before I was injured, friends and family seem much more willing to share theirs,” he says. “When I think about how I might have come across before, serving naval officer, Olympian, looking a certain way, maybe that’s not conducive to getting to know people. They feel safer with me now, a whole different level of interaction from 6ft 6ins to being 4ft 11ins.”
He reflects on all the time he spent with Paralympians during his years as an elite rower. “I miss being 6ft 6ins and having strong legs and all the other cool things that come with being able-bodied, but I was a bit ignorant then, too,” he says.
“I was living with [Paralympians] Tom Aggar, Helene Raynsford, Rachel Morris and their spinal-cord injuries. I did not know enough about it, shame on me. Tom is now my spinal-injury mentor, but back then I did not ask all the questions, ‘Explain this, how should I handle that. . .’”
He has had to learn his own limitations. Typically, he battled every day during 18 months at a naval rehabilitation institute to be “the best patient in the world”, but accepts that he will not be walking again. He strains to lift one leg a few inches to kick the table.
The contrast from that day in 2012, powering his boat to victory, could make him sad, but he fills up with pride. “The stories you hear of where people were, what they were doing,” he says. “Royal Navy ships came into areas so they could get a signal to watch, even submarines surfaced.”
He holds his gold medal. “Didn’t we get it right that summer?” Reed adds. “People will be talking about it for decades. They will be telling their grandchildren. I have heard thousands of those stories in the past 10 years. It is amazing. Yes, it was expensive to stage, but think about the huge amounts of money we have wasted on things that have given us a lot less pleasure and unity. After the past couple of years, with so much isolation, how do you put a price on something that brought so many people together?” As he says, no regrets.
